plan.title: Intro to Rocket Science: Push, Mass & Orbit
plan.hook: Follow the connection between exhaust momentum, changing vehicle mass and the sideways speed needed for orbit.
objectives: Explain rocket thrust without air to push against.
Use the ideal rocket equation with its assumptions.
Distinguish reaching altitude from reaching orbit.
prerequisites: Ratios; logarithms are introduced in context

sections.heading: Orbit is falling with enough sideways speed
points: Orbital weightlessness comes from shared free fall, not absent gravity.
Sustained orbit requires suitable sideways motion as well as altitude.
Without enough sideways speed, gravity brings the object back down rather than curving its path around Earth.

sections.heading: Exhaust momentum pushes the vehicle
sections.body:
A rocket accelerates exhaust backward and gains forward momentum. It does not need atmospheric air to push against. A chemical rocket carries fuel and oxidiser, allowing combustion to continue in a vacuum when its engine is designed for those conditions.

In a simplified case where nozzle exit pressure matches ambient pressure, thrust F equals mass flow rate ṁ times exhaust speed ve relative to the rocket: F = ṁve. Here F is in newtons, ṁ in kilograms per second, and ve in metres per second. Ejecting 5 kg/s at 2,000 m/s gives 10,000 N of thrust. Real nozzle pressure differences add another term.

Thrust is only one force on a launching vehicle. Near Earth, gravity pulls downward and atmospheric drag can resist motion. A vertical vehicle initially lifts only if the upward thrust exceeds its weight and other opposing forces; producing thrust alone does not guarantee a successful launch.
sections.visual: Exhaust carries momentum backward while the rocket gains momentum forward. The engine exchanges momentum with its propellant, so it can work in a vacuum.

questions.q: Why can a rocket work in a vacuum?
questions.answer: The rocket pushes on its own exhaust, which carries momentum backward. It does not require surrounding air as a reaction surface.

sections.heading: Propellant changes the mass you accelerate
sections.body:
As a rocket uses propellant, its mass decreases. The ideal rocket equation accounts for that changing mass: Δv = ve ln(m0/mf). Delta-v means the ideal change in velocity; ve is effective exhaust speed, m0 is initial total mass, mf is final total mass, and ln is the natural logarithm. The mass ratio inside the logarithm has no units.

With ve = 3,000 m/s and m0/mf = 2, Δv is approximately 3,000 × 0.693 = 2,080 m/s. Increasing the ratio to 4 gives approximately 4,160 m/s. Doubling mass ratio does not double the logarithm in general; these values follow the logarithm's specific relationship.

This ideal model assumes constant effective exhaust speed and omits external-force losses. A real ascent must budget gravity and drag losses plus manoeuvring needs. Final mass includes structure and payload, not just an empty fuel container. Staging helps by discarding structure that no longer contributes to the remaining flight.
sections.visual: Propellant leaves the vehicle during a burn, so the mass being accelerated decreases. In the ideal rocket equation, delta-v depends on effective exhaust speed and the logarithm of initial mass divided by final mass.

questions.q: Does the ideal rocket equation directly give altitude?
questions.hint: Check the units of its output.
questions.answer: No. It gives an ideal velocity change in metres per second. Altitude depends on the trajectory, gravity, drag and timing of thrust.

sections.heading: Orbit is falling with enough sideways speed
sections.body:
Reaching a high altitude is different from staying in orbit. An orbiting object is continuously falling under gravity while moving sideways fast enough that its path curves around Earth. Gravity remains substantial in low Earth orbit; astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are in free fall together.

A circular orbit near Earth requires a speed roughly around 7.8 km/s, with the exact value depending on altitude. This is an approximate orbital speed, not a launch vehicle's complete delta-v budget. A straight upward launch without suitable sideways motion can rise high and then fall back.

An ideal orbit above significant atmospheric drag does not need continuous thrust merely to continue moving. Real spacecraft may perform corrections and compensate for drag. Mission planning must also control orbital plane, altitude and encounter timing. “Get high enough” leaves most of the navigation problem unsolved.
sections.visual: The amber arrow is tangent to this circular orbit and shows sideways velocity. The green arrow points toward Earth and shows gravitational acceleration. Both arrows turn with the satellite; gravity continuously bends its path.

questions.q: Why is a very high vertical jump not automatically an orbit?
questions.answer: Without enough sideways speed, gravity brings the object back down rather than curving its path around Earth.

questions.q: Ignoring the pressure term, 5 kg/s of exhaust at 2,000 m/s gives what thrust?
questions.explain: F = ṁve = 5 × 2,000 = 10,000 N. The units kg/s × m/s give kg·m/s², or newtons.

questions.q: What does a chemical rocket carry that lets combustion work without atmospheric oxygen?
questions.explain: A chemical rocket carries an oxidiser as well as fuel. Wings and atmospheric drag are not required for its momentum-exchange principle.

questions.q: At ve = 3,000 m/s and mass ratio 2, what is approximate ideal delta-v?
questions.explain: Use 3,000 × ln(2), with ln(2) ≈ 0.693, to obtain about 2,080 m/s.

questions.q: What belongs in the final mass mf?
choices: Remaining structure and payload, plus anything else still carried
questions.explain: Final mass is what the vehicle still carries after the burn. Treating structure and payload as massless would exaggerate capability.

questions.q: Why do astronauts float in an orbiting spacecraft?
choices: They and the spacecraft fall together
The engine always pushes them upward
questions.explain: They share orbital free fall. Gravity is still what bends the path around Earth.

questions.q: What distinguishes a basic orbit from simply reaching a high point?
questions.explain: Orbit depends on velocity and trajectory, not altitude alone. Gravity remains essential to the curved motion.
